title: Tips needed for agentic system for my game
author: Decent_Departure9874
selftext:
Hi, i have currently made a game using Unity and claude code. I am amazed how well it works.

I have limited time soon to work on the game, but want to keep improving it. Therefore i want to setup an agentic system. So far is work with 1-3 claude code terminals at the same time, which is very effective, but i need to stay in the loop.

I want to implement something, where i have some sort of product manager agent, who will look at my backlog/notes and command other agents (e.g. code, design, etc.) to build stuff. Ideally i interact with it minimally,  only for key decisions and human testing. Any tips? Want to start with a simple, but effective setup first

replies.author: Decent_Departure9874
replies.body: Well, the goal is to set this up well, to avoid generating slop

replies.author: YKLKTMA
replies.body: AI is incapable of producing anything other than slop; the more automation you introduce into game design, the more garbage will be created.

replies.author: Decent_Departure9874
replies.body: I think this is top blunt. If you give the right instructions, guardrails, and make things concrete it works. Just need to find the right loop

replies.author: YKLKTMA
replies.body: It is impossible to automatically create a good game; that is an illusion. AI does not possess intelligence, it simply makes statistical guesses about each subsequent token, producing whatever the statistics dictate. AI is like a hammer: it can drive nails, but it cannot design a house. If you don’t have the time, you should do something else; you won’t be able to make a game anyway, as the process will inevitably require months or even years of iteration.

replies.author: Decent_Departure9874
replies.body: Party agree; AI is just a texy generator in a way..however, if i give clear direction and ideas, AI should be able to execute. My main goal is to minimize my involvement, and put my scarce time into the design, and let AI handle the full implementation and partly the testing

replies.author: YKLKTMA
replies.body:
This won’t work; there literally isn’t a single halfway-decent game created by AI. Don’t harbor any illusions about this, no matter how hard you try to achieve something else, AI will only ever generate slop.

The key to success lies in iterating on the design, playtesting with the target audience, processing feedback, and then refining the design once more, none of this is something AI can help with.

comments.author: Lola_Montezz
comments.body:
Not sure to what extent you have an engineering background (not necessary per se), but here are my non-negotiables:

- Create a .claude folder in your repo with a CLAUDE.md file. (Look up if you don't know what that is) In here, you can explain what your game is, what genre, inspired by, the goal, etc. Maybe 1-2 paragraphs at most. The second thing that this file (and your project) NEEDS are: linters, formatters, tests. You add command line instruction examples on how to run those. Important to know: every line you write in this file **always** gets sent with your conversations.

- Create Skills (look up if you don't know what that is) for specific workflow instructions. Need to add an item? Document the work process here. Document the style if it's modelling, document the relevant classes to add them to your game, etc. Important to know: **Claude decides** if a Skill should be used or not. No guarantees, but you can write a description on when Claude should call it in the metadata, and mention in your CLAUDE.md to check for relevant Skills.

The cool thing about Skills is that they can be created or modified by your agents as well. Essentially if you work on a new feature, you could have Claude take its own notes to achieve a more hands-off approach. 

My general advice is to start reading up on what kind of AI artifacts you can configure for Claude, because rawdogging without these leads to either terribly generic results or just straight up slop. Gl!

comments.author: cheyumaama
comments.body: You'll just be burning through your money for nothing. Game development is art. AI doesn't make good art when left to its own intelligence

comments.author: forgingtheflow
comments.body:
I spent over 3 weeks working with Claude on my game idea. Every spare minute i had, I gave it every idea I wanted to see in the game. It was a game I’ve wanted to make for years. Every idea Claude audited them to reduce any gaps or inconsistencies and ran the scenarios in a simulation.  
230,000 words, roughly 460 pages. 

That was just the handover documents for the coding session.

Brother you will make slop if you don’t have a solid plan.

replies.author: Decent_Departure9874
replies.body:
You mean, you created a 460 page document with all the specific of your game, and used those 460 pages with Claude to actually build it?
I think this makes sense. Get very clear and concrete what you want first, then build. However, how did you handle the implementation/building of the game with claude?

replies.author: forgingtheflow
replies.body: Forgive me if I misunderstood your question about implementation: what I did was a Claude code session, handed it the files and said please read through and let me know if you have any questions. I used ultracode because I want the quality control it offers. Basically the handover was set up so Claude code could just start. It had no questions so I said, ‘Please start.’ The document was to have as little friction as possible.

replies.author: Decent_Departure9874
replies.body: Nice! How did you create the document? I currently break everything down in clear phases, to avoid geving too big tasks. How did you manage that?

replies.author: forgingtheflow
replies.body:
I used Claude cowork, so I could access it from my phone at work (shhh). I started by telling it I wanted to make a game, and sharing ideas from XY game and ZY game, and mentioned what elements I liked. I let it search up those games and respond. Then I walked it through the differences my game was going to have, so an overall view / high-level view of the game. I let it take in my ideas and record and ask questions regularly. I gave it every idea I had, I just kept throwing them at it in no particular order. The hardest part that was beyond my abilities was the economy part of the game, I had to copy and paste what the other games were doing numbers-wise so Claude could formulate how to balance my game. Then it would start running simulations on the numbers and let me know where the economy was failing, etc. We started with a dozen resources and eventually it grew to over 250. We kept adding different segments / batches to be simulated.   
When I had nothing left to add to the handover, I ran this part on the highest effort level.
